Folks — ran the matrix overnight and attached the raw CSV (redwood-map-benchmark-results-20270418.csv). Highlights and interpretation below (all numbers median unless noted):

Model: transformer-13B (128-token prompt)
- A100-80GB (full GPU): TTFT = 38 ms, p50 token latency = 9 ms, p95 token latency = 36 ms, throughput ~ 2200 tokens/sec at concurrency=4, 1800 tps at concurrency=8, 1200 tps at concurrency=16.
- H100-80GB (full GPU): TTFT = 28 ms, p50 = 7 ms, p95 = 28 ms, throughput ~ 3100 tps @4, 2700 @8, 2100 @16. Noticeably better p95 and sustained throughput due to sparsity/kernels for fp16/faster attention.
- L40S-48GB (full GPU): TTFT = 34 ms, p50 = 8 ms, p95 = 40 ms, throughput ~ 2000 @4, 1600 @8, 1100 @16. Cost lower per-hour than H100 but p95 higher under bursty load.

MIG (density) runs — 2-way MIG where available (A100 and H100):
- A100 2-way MIG: TTFT = 52 ms, p95 = 62 ms, throughput per MIG slice ~ 950 tps @4 (aggregate better density but large tail).
- H100 2-way MIG: TTFT = 42 ms, p95 = 48 ms, throughput per slice ~ 1400 tps @4.

Observations:
- H100 gives the best single-instance TTFT and p95; for latency-sensitive endpoints H100 is the clean winner.
- MIG delivers cost-efficient density for low-latency non-tail-sensitive workloads (e.g., batch embedding pipelines or internal tooling). But MIG increases TTFT and widens p95 tails in our tests.
- L40S is attractive for cost-constrained read-heavy workloads but shows higher tail latency under concurrency.

Sizing recommendation (assuming target steady-state 1000 qps equivalent, 13B model):
- Low-latency SLO (p95 <= 50 ms): 4x H100-80GB nodes (redundant across AZs) — supports steady-state and 2x headroom for bursts.
- Cost-optimized with acceptable p95 (~60-80ms): 6x A100-80GB (or 8x L40S-48GB) with batching tuned; consider 2-way MIG for internal batch jobs only.

Next steps: I can produce a one-page PDF with a simple cost delta chart (H100 vs A100 vs L40S) and final recommended commit tiers.

— Marcus
